title: Multiplication Tables 1 to 10 for Grade 3: The Order to Learn Them + Free Quiz
meta_title: Multiplication Tables 1 to 10 Grade 3 + Free Quiz
meta_desc: Learn multiplication tables 1 to 10 in Grade 3 the smart way: the order to memorise, patterns for each table and a free 8-question quiz. Try it now.
excerpt: There are not 100 facts to memorise in the tables 1 to 10 — there are far fewer. Here is the order I teach the tables in, the pattern that makes each one stick, and a quick quiz to test recall.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Watch a Grade 3 child meet the times tables for the first time and you can almost see the panic: a wall of 100 facts, from 1 × 1 all the way to 10 × 10, that apparently must all be crammed into memory. That is the wrong picture, and it is why so many children dread this stage. The truth is that mastering multiplication tables 1 to 10 in Grade 3 means learning far fewer facts than 100 — and learning them in an order where each new table leans on the ones before it.

I have taught this to eight-year-olds in classrooms and to my own nephew at a kitchen table in Jaipur, and the same sequence works every time. It is not the 1, 2, 3, 4… order printed in most textbooks. Here is the order that actually sticks, and why.

Why multiplication tables 1 to 10 are smaller than they look

Start with the single most useful idea in the whole topic: 4 × 7 and 7 × 4 give the same answer. This is the commutative property, and children do not need the word — they need the consequence. Every time you learn one fact, you get its mirror free. That one insight roughly halves the facts left to memorise.

Add the easy tables (the 1s, the 10s, and much of the 2s and 5s), and the genuinely hard set shrinks to a small handful. In my experience the whole of ‘difficult’ multiplication for a Grade 3 child comes down to about eight or nine facts, mostly hiding in the 7s and 8s.

The order to learn the tables

Do not march through 1 to 10 in numerical order. Teach the anchor tables first — the ones with the strongest patterns — then use them to reach the rest.

  • Start with 2, 5 and 10. These have the clearest patterns and give a child early wins. The 10s are just the number with a zero after it; the 5s end in 5, 0, 5, 0; the 2s are doubles they may already know from addition.
  • Then the 1s and 0s. Anything times 1 is itself; anything times 0 is 0. Two rules, a whole row of facts gone.
  • Then the squares: 3 × 3, 4 × 4, 6 × 6, 7 × 7, 8 × 8, 9 × 9. Squares are memorable because both numbers match, and they act as landmarks — once you know 6 × 6 = 36, you can reach 6 × 7 with one more group.
  • Then 3, 4 and 6, building on doubling: the 4s are double the 2s, the 6s are double the 3s.
  • Finish with the tricky ones — 7 and 8. By now most of their facts are already learned as mirrors (7 × 5 came free with the 5s, 8 × 2 came with the 2s). Only a few genuinely new facts remain.

Patterns that make each table easier

Rote chanting has its place, but a child who sees the pattern remembers longer and recovers faster when a fact slips. These are the patterns I point out explicitly.

TablePattern to noticeExample
2Doubling — same as adding the number to itself2 × 8 = 8 + 8 = 16
5Answers end in 5, 0, 5, 0; half of the 10s5 × 6 = half of 60 = 30
9Digits add to 9; tens digit is one less than the multiplier9 × 4 = 36 (3 + 6 = 9)
10Just write the number and add a zero10 × 7 = 70
4Double, then double again4 × 6 = double 12 = 24

The 9s finger trick, honestly assessed

You may have seen the trick where you fold down a finger to read off the 9 times table. It works, and children love it. My honest caveat: treat it as a bridge, not a destination. A child who relies on it for 9 × 6 in a timed test is slower than one who simply knows 54. Use the trick to build confidence, then quietly retire it.

Skip-counting: the bridge to recall

Before facts become instant, they pass through skip-counting. Counting ‘3, 6, 9, 12, 15…’ is multiplication in slow motion, and it is the honest way a child works out 3 × 5 before it is memorised. Encourage it early, out loud, even in the car. But be clear with yourself about the goal: skip-counting is the scaffold, not the finished building. The aim is for 3 × 5 to come back in under three seconds without the child counting up to it.

How to practise for speed and recall

Fluency is recall under a mild time pressure, and it comes from short, frequent practice — not marathon sessions the night before a test.

  • Five minutes daily beats an hour on Sunday. Pick one table, do a quick mix of facts, move on.
  • Practise the mirrors together. Learn 6 × 7 and 7 × 6 as one thing, not two.
  • Mix the order. A child who can only recite a table in sequence has memorised a song, not the facts. Ask 8 × 4 straight after 8 × 9.
  • Target the weak facts. Most children have four or five specific facts they trip on — often 7 × 8 and 6 × 8. Drill those, not the ones already secure.

One counter-intuitive point worth remembering: a child who reasons out 7 × 8 = 56 from 7 × 7 = 49 in five seconds is in a stronger position than one who blurts a memorised answer but cannot check it. Understanding first, speed second. Speed always follows.

quiz.title: Grade 3 Multiplication Tables 1 to 10 Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight quick questions across the tables 1 to 10. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.

questions.explanation: 6 × 7 = 42. If you know 6 × 6 = 36, add one more 6 to get 42.
The 5s end in 5 or 0. 8 × 5 = 40, which is half of 8 × 10 = 80.
For the 9s the digits add to 9: 3 + 6 = 9, so 9 × 4 = 36.

questions.q: Which fact gives the same answer as 7 × 3?
questions.explanation: Order does not change the product, so 7 × 3 and 3 × 7 both equal 21.
7 × 8 = 56. This is one of the trickiest facts, so it is worth extra drilling.
For the 10s, write the number and add a zero: 10 × 6 = 60.
This is a square. Double 4 is 8, and double 8 is 16, so 4 × 4 = 16.

faq.q: In what order should a Grade 3 child learn the tables?
faq.a: Not 1 to 10 in sequence. Start with 2, 5 and 10 for early wins, then 1 and 0, then the squares (3×3, 4×4 and so on), then 3, 4 and 6 by doubling, and finish with the tricky 7s and 8s — most of which are already learned as mirror facts by then.

faq.q: How many multiplication facts must a child actually memorise?
faq.a: Far fewer than 100. Because 4 × 7 equals 7 × 4, learning one fact gives you its mirror free, which roughly halves the set. Add the easy 1s, 10s, 2s and 5s and the genuinely hard facts come down to about eight or nine.

faq.q: Is skip-counting good or a bad habit?
faq.a: It is a good bridge, not the destination. Skip-counting is how a child works out 3 × 5 before it is memorised. Encourage it early, but aim for the fact to come back in under three seconds without counting up to it.

faq.q: Which facts do children find hardest?
faq.a: Usually a small set in the 7s and 8s — 7 × 8 and 6 × 8 are classic stumbling blocks. Rather than re-drilling tables a child already knows, target these specific weak facts.
